subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis threshold at the time of starting antiretroviral therapy
stem:
You are the registrar in an infectious diseases clinic seeing a 36 year old man diagnosed with HIV three weeks ago after presenting with oral thrush and six months of intermittent night sweats.

He feels reasonably well and has no cough, breathlessness, headache or visual symptoms. His chest radiograph is clear and his examination is unremarkable apart from the treated oral candidiasis. His baseline bloods are back and antiretroviral therapy is being started today. He has no drug allergies, and his glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity is normal.

data_table.Immune status: CD4 count 140 cells/microlitre, HIV viral load 180000 copies/mL
data_table.Other results: Full blood count and renal function within normal limits, chest radiograph clear, toxoplasma and cryptococcal antigen negative
data_table.Allergies: No known drug allergies, normal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity

lead_in: Which additional treatment should be started alongside his antiretroviral therapy?

options.text: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole as prophylaxis against pneumocystis
options.rationale: Prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii is indicated once the CD4 count falls below 200 cells per microlitre, and his count of 140 places him clearly within that group. It is continued until the count has been sustained above 200 for at least three months on effective antiretroviral therapy. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV management guidelines)

options.text: Weekly azithromycin as prophylaxis against mycobacterial infection
options.rationale: Prophylaxis against disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex is considered at a CD4 count below 50 cells per microlitre, well below his current level. It is also increasingly omitted when effective antiretroviral therapy is started promptly. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV management guidelines)

options.text: No prophylaxis until the CD4 count falls below fifty cells per microlitre
options.rationale: This applies the threshold for a different organism and would leave him unprotected through the period of greatest pneumocystis risk. The 200 cell threshold is the one that governs here. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV management guidelines)

options.text: Fluconazole as continuing prophylaxis against recurrent fungal disease
options.rationale: Antifungal prophylaxis is not routine because of resistance selection and interactions, and his candidiasis has already been treated as an acute episode. Recurrence is managed with repeat treatment rather than continuous suppression in most patients. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV management guidelines)

options.text: No prophylaxis at all because antiretroviral therapy is being started
options.rationale: The CD4 count takes months to recover after antiretroviral therapy begins, leaving a window of continuing vulnerability during which pneumocystis pneumonia commonly presents. Prophylaxis covers precisely that interval. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV management guidelines)

explanation.summary: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis in HIV is governed by CD4 count thresholds that should be committed to memory, because they determine what is started and when it can safely stop. Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis begins below 200 cells per microlitre, or in the presence of oropharyngeal candidiasis or an AIDS defining illness, and trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is the agent of choice since it also covers toxoplasmosis at higher doses. Toxoplasma prophylaxis is added below 100 cells per microlitre in seropositive patients, and Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis is considered below 50, although it is increasingly omitted when antiretroviral therapy is commenced promptly. Prophylaxis is stopped once the CD4 count has been sustained above the relevant threshold for at least three months on suppressive therapy. Patients starting treatment at low counts should also be warned about immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, in which recovering immunity unmasks or worsens an underlying infection in the first weeks.
key_points: Pneumocystis prophylaxis starts below 200 cells per microlitre
Toxoplasma prophylaxis is added below 100 in seropositive patients
Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis is considered below 50
Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole covers both pneumocystis and toxoplasma
Stop prophylaxis after three months sustained above the threshold on therapy
explanation.pearls: Pneumocystis pneumonia characteristically shows marked exertional desaturation with a chest radiograph that looks far better than the patient, so a normal film never excludes it in someone with a CD4 count below 200.

subtopic_detail: Adjunct that reduces recurrence in a first episode of acute pericarditis
stem:
A 32 year old man presents to the emergency department where you are the registrar, with two days of sharp central chest pain that is worse when he lies flat and eases when he sits forward. He had a viral upper respiratory illness a fortnight ago.

He is haemodynamically stable and comfortable sitting up. On auscultation you hear a scratchy sound over the left sternal edge that varies with his position. His troponin taken on arrival and repeated at three hours are both within normal limits, and a bedside echocardiogram shows normal ventricular function with no pericardial collection. He has been started on regular ibuprofen with good effect. He takes no regular medication and his renal function is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Scratchy friction rub at the left sternal edge varying with position, no pulsus paradoxus, jugular venous pressure not elevated
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Widespread concave upward ST elevation with PR segment depression, reciprocal changes in aVR
data_table.Investigations: Serial troponin within normal limits, C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), echocardiogram shows normal function with no effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?

options.text: Add prednisolone at moderate dose and taper it over four weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroids provide rapid symptom relief but are associated with a higher rate of recurrence, so they are reserved for patients who cannot take anti inflammatories or colchicine, or where an autoimmune cause is established. Using them first makes the disease more likely to come back. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Add a proton pump inhibitor and continue the anti inflammatory alone
options.rationale: Gastric protection is sensible alongside a nonsteroidal anti inflammatory but does nothing to reduce recurrence, which is the main long term problem in this condition. It addresses a side effect rather than the disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Start therapeutic anticoagulation and admit for cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Anticoagulation has no role and theoretically risks haemorrhagic transformation of a pericardial effusion. He also lacks any high risk feature such as fever above 38 degrees, a large effusion, tamponade or immunosuppression that would mandate admission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Arrange urgent coronary angiography before any further treatment
options.rationale: The widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, positional pain, friction rub and normal serial troponin describe a pericardial rather than a coronary process. Angiography would be indicated if the ST elevation were territorial with a rising troponin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Add colchicine to the anti inflammatory and continue for three months
options.rationale: Colchicine added to a nonsteroidal anti inflammatory approximately halves the rate of recurrent pericarditis and shortens symptom duration, which is why it is recommended for a first episode rather than held back for recurrence. A three month course is standard for an initial episode, extended to six months if the condition recurs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed on two of four features comprising characteristic positional pleuritic chest pain, a friction rub, widespread ST elevation with PR depression, and a new or worsening pericardial effusion. Most cases in Australian practice are viral or idiopathic and can be managed as an outpatient, with admission reserved for high risk features such as fever above 38 degrees, subacute onset, a large effusion or tamponade, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, trauma or failure to respond after a week of treatment. A raised troponin indicates myopericardial involvement and warrants admission and echocardiography, which changes the advice about exercise restriction. Treatment is a nonsteroidal anti inflammatory with colchicine, the latter now standard from the first episode because randomised evidence shows it roughly halves recurrence, and corticosteroids are deliberately avoided first line because they increase it.
key_points: Diagnosis needs two of four: positional pain, rub, typical ECG changes, effusion
Colchicine from the first episode roughly halves the recurrence rate
Corticosteroids relieve symptoms quickly but increase recurrence
A raised troponin indicates myopericarditis and changes management
Exercise restriction is advised until symptoms and markers normalise
explanation.pearls: PR segment depression is the most specific electrocardiographic sign of pericarditis and is the feature that most reliably separates it from the territorial ST elevation of an occluded coronary artery.

subtopic_detail: Transfusion strategy for acute chest syndrome with hypoxia during a vaso-occlusive admission
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward to review a 24 year old woman with homozygous sickle cell disease who was admitted three days ago with severe limb and back pain and is receiving opioid analgesia.

Overnight she developed a fever and pleuritic chest pain, and this morning she is breathless at rest and needing increasing oxygen. Her chest radiograph, which was clear on admission, now shows new consolidation involving two lobes. Her haemoglobin has fallen from her documented baseline and her reticulocyte count is high. Intravenous antibiotics have been commenced and the haematology consultant is on her way in.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 88% on 6 L/min oxygen, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 62 g/L (115-155), baseline documented at 88 g/L, platelets 148 x10^9/L (150-400), reticulocytes elevated
data_table.Imaging: New consolidation involving two lobes on chest radiograph, clear on admission
data_table.Treatment so far: Intravenous antibiotics commenced, opioid analgesia continuing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate transfusion strategy?

options.text: Simple top up transfusion of two units with continued oxygen therapy
options.rationale: Simple transfusion is appropriate for milder acute chest syndrome or symptomatic anaemia without hypoxia, and it raises the haemoglobin without efficiently lowering the proportion of sickled cells. Raising the haematocrit alone can also increase viscosity and worsen vaso-occlusion. (Source: HSANZ: Sickle cell disease management)

options.text: Intravenous fluids at twice maintenance with continued opioid analgesia
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid loading in a patient with multilobar consolidation and hypoxia risks pulmonary oedema and worsening gas exchange, and analgesia alone does not treat the process in the lung. Over hydration is a recognised contributor to deterioration in this syndrome. (Source: HSANZ: Sickle cell disease management)

options.text: Urgent exchange transfusion with respiratory support and antibiotics
options.rationale: Severe acute chest syndrome with hypoxia and multilobar involvement requires exchange transfusion, which rapidly reduces the proportion of haemoglobin S without increasing blood viscosity, unlike simple transfusion. It is combined with oxygen or higher levels of respiratory support, antibiotics covering atypical organisms, careful fluid balance and incentive spirometry. (Source: HSANZ: Sickle cell disease management)

options.text: Hydroxyurea started immediately with continued supportive care
options.rationale: Hydroxyurea raises foetal haemoglobin and reduces the frequency of future crises and chest syndrome episodes, but it takes weeks to months to work and has no role in an acute deterioration. It should be discussed for secondary prevention after recovery. (Source: HSANZ: Sickle cell disease management)

options.text: Therapeutic anticoagulation for presumed pulmonary thromboembolism
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism does occur at higher rates in this population and deserves consideration, but fever with new consolidation developing during a painful crisis is the classic pattern of acute chest syndrome. Anticoagulating without treating the underlying sickling would miss the actual process. (Source: HSANZ: Sickle cell disease management)

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death in adults with sickle cell disease and is defined by a new pulmonary infiltrate with fever or respiratory symptoms. It typically develops two to three days into an admission for a vaso-occlusive crisis, which makes it a complication to anticipate actively rather than await, and the mechanisms combine infection, pulmonary fat embolism from infarcted marrow, and hypoventilation from chest wall pain and opioid analgesia. Management comprises oxygen and escalating respiratory support, antibiotics that cover atypical organisms, cautious fluid balance, adequate analgesia and incentive spirometry to counter splinting. The transfusion decision turns on severity: simple transfusion suffices for milder disease, while hypoxia, multilobar involvement or clinical deterioration calls for exchange transfusion, which lowers the haemoglobin S fraction without the viscosity penalty of simply adding red cells.
key_points: New infiltrate with fever or respiratory symptoms defines the syndrome
It commonly develops two to three days into a vaso-occlusive admission
Opioid induced hypoventilation and chest splinting are contributors
Exchange transfusion is used for hypoxia, multilobar disease or deterioration
Incentive spirometry during painful crises reduces the incidence
explanation.pearls: Incentive spirometry prescribed routinely during a vaso-occlusive crisis reduces the incidence of acute chest syndrome, making it one of the few genuinely preventive bedside interventions in this disease.

subtopic_detail: Treatment of raised intracranial pressure with papilloedema and normal neuroimaging
stem:
A 28 year old woman is referred to your general medical clinic with four months of daily headache that is worst when she first wakes and when she bends forward. She has also noticed brief greying of vision in both eyes when she stands up quickly, lasting a few seconds each time.

She describes a whooshing sound in both ears in time with her pulse. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she has gained 14 kg over two years. She takes no medication other than the combined oral contraceptive pill and has never taken tetracyclines or vitamin A derivatives. Fundoscopy shows bilateral swollen optic discs with blurred margins. Formal visual field testing shows an enlarged blind spot on both sides with otherwise preserved fields.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema, no focal neurological deficit, no meningism, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and magnetic resonance venography both reported as normal with no mass, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosis
data_table.Lumbar puncture: Opening pressure 32 cmH2O, cerebrospinal fluid cell count, protein and glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures as the mainstay of treatment
options.rationale: Pressure reverts within hours of drainage so repeated punctures give only transient relief, and the procedure is uncomfortable and carries its own risks. It is used as a temporising measure in pregnancy or while awaiting surgery rather than as ongoing treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Acetazolamide with weight management and visual field monitoring
options.rationale: Acetazolamide reduces cerebrospinal fluid production through carbonic anhydrase inhibition and is the first line drug, with randomised evidence supporting its combination with weight reduction for improving visual field outcomes. Serial perimetry is essential because visual loss rather than headache determines the need to escalate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Referral for urgent optic nerve sheath fenestration this admission
options.rationale: Surgical decompression is reserved for rapidly progressive or severe visual loss that threatens sight despite medical therapy, and her acuity and fields are currently preserved apart from an enlarged blind spot. Proceeding now would expose her to operative risk without indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Prednisolone at high dose with a slow taper over three months
options.rationale: Corticosteroids produce rebound elevation of pressure on withdrawal and contribute to the weight gain that drives the condition, so they are not used for maintenance. They are occasionally used briefly as a bridge before urgent surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Topiramate alone with review of the headache in three months
options.rationale: Topiramate has weak carbonic anhydrase activity and assists with weight loss, making it a reasonable second line or adjunctive option, but the evidence base favours acetazolamide first. Reviewing only at three months would also miss deteriorating fields. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects women of reproductive age with a raised body mass index and recent weight gain, and presents with headache that is worse on waking and on bending, pulsatile tinnitus and transient visual obscurations. Diagnosis follows the modified Dandy criteria: signs and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure, no focal neurological deficit other than a sixth nerve palsy, normal neuroimaging including venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, a raised opening pressure on lumbar puncture, and normal cerebrospinal fluid constituents. The threat is to vision rather than to life, and papilloedema can progress to irreversible optic atrophy while the headache is unremarkable, so serial formal perimetry rather than symptom report drives management. Treatment combines acetazolamide with sustained weight reduction, and offending drugs including tetracyclines, retinoids and excess vitamin A are stopped where relevant.
key_points: Venography is required to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Normal cerebrospinal fluid constituents with a raised opening pressure are required
Vision rather than headache determines urgency and escalation
Acetazolamide with weight reduction is first line therapy
Serial formal visual field testing is the key monitoring tool
explanation.pearls: A sixth nerve palsy is the only focal deficit permitted by the diagnostic criteria, because it is a false localising sign produced by the raised pressure itself rather than evidence of a structural lesion.

sources.label: RANZCO: Papilloedema and idiopathic intracranial hypertension
